56-006.r: Macaroni wheat → Triticum durum: tetraploid; second most cultivated wheat after common wheat, yet only about 5-10% of global wheat production.

56-007.r: Parthenium hysterophorus leaf extract → used for biologically synthesized nanoparticles (eco-friendly technology); shows anti-cancer property.

56-008.r: Litmus (acid-base indicator) → water-soluble mix of dyes extracted from lichens; one of the oldest pH indicators.

56-009.r: Neem: its oil (azadirachtin) works as a pesticide on some insects and mites and has pharmaceutical uses (1 and 3 true); statement 2 is false.

56-010.r: Pine, fir, spruce, cedar, larch, cypress (timber trees of hills) → gymnosperms, 'naked seeds' – seeds not enclosed.

56-011.r: Mushrooms: some are medicinal, some psychoactive, some insecticidal, some bioluminescent – all four statements correct.

56-012.r: Aloe vera → medicinal crop (antiviral, antibacterial); sugarcane → sugar; cotton → fibre; mahua → flowers for food and wine, seed oil.

56-013.r: Tulsi (Ocimum tenuiflorum or sanctum, holy basil, family Lamiaceae) → medicinal due to phenols and flavonoids (antiseptic, antimicrobial, antioxidant).

56-014.r: Palm oil is a raw material for lipstick and perfumes and can make biodiesel (2, 3 true); oil palm is not native to Southeast Asia but to west Africa.

56-015.r: National Policy on Biofuels 2018 raw materials: cassava, damaged wheat grains, rotten potatoes, sugar beet (1, 2, 5, 6); not groundnut seeds or horse gram.

56-016.r: Three pairs correct: cassava – woody shrub; ginger – herb with pseudostem; Malabar spinach – herbaceous climber. Mint and papaya pairs are wrong.

56-017.r: USA is the largest ethanol producer, Brazil second (Statement I wrong); USA uses corn, Brazil sugarcane as main feedstock (II correct); together 80% of world ethanol.

56-018.r: Canola → edible oil bred from rapeseed (University of Manitoba, Canada, early 1970s); key trait: very low erucic acid; low saturated fat.

56-019.r: Correct (3, 4, 5): most Indian tamarind is minor forest produce; India exports tamarind and moringa seeds; both seeds can make biofuel. Moringa is not leguminous.

56-020.r: Only one is native to India (red sanders); cashew came from Brazil (Portuguese, via Goa) and papaya from tropical America (southern Mexico).

56-021.r: Fourth generation biofuels → genetically modified microorganisms such as algae (also yeast, fungi, cyanobacteria) that photosynthesize CO2 into fuel.

56-022.r: Pongam (Pongamia pinnata) → leguminous petro-plant; its seed oil is used as biodiesel and for skin disease.

56-023.r: Petro-crops (e.g. Jatropha) → yield biofuel such as biodiesel; rich in hydrocarbons and lipids.

56-024.r: India's first biodiesel plant → Kakinada, Andhra Pradesh.

56-025.r: Bio-diesel plant → Jatropha curcas: non-edible angiosperm, grows in harsh land with little water; its seeds give biodiesel.

56-028.r: Ethanol biofuel → sugarcane: made by fermenting sugarcane juice and molasses; a clean, low-carbon transport fuel.

56-029.r: Molasses (from sugarcane juice) → excellent raw material for power alcohol.

56-030.r: Chilgoza → seeds of pine (Pinus gerardiana); rich in carbohydrate and protein.

56-031.r: Chief mosquito repellent → neem (margo); tulsi and turmeric have antibiotic quality; lemon gives vitamin C.

56-032.r: Brahmi → brain tonic; sadabahar → anti-diabetic; pudina → carminative (relieves gas); tulsi → expectorant.

56-033.r: Colas contain significant caffeine (added during manufacture; natural in tea and coffee); caffeine = xanthine alkaloid stimulant that reduces fatigue.

56-034.r: Caffeine (alkaloid stimulant) is present in both tea and coffee, also in cocoa and cola drinks.

56-035.r: Most important stimulant in tea leaves → caffeine, the world's most widely consumed CNS stimulant (from tea leaves and coffee beans).

56-036.r: Seaweeds (marine algae) → richest natural source of iodine.

56-037.r: All three are plant products: camphor (wood of camphor laurel, Cinnamomum camphora), chicory (herb with blue flowers) and vanilla.

56-038.r: Kuttu flour → buckwheat (Fagopyrum esculentum), a pseudocereal; not related to wheat as it is not a grass.

56-039.r: Saffron spice → dried stigmas (with styles) of the Crocus sativus flower; each flower has three crimson stigmas.

56-040.r: Peppermint oil → mainly from leaves (steam distillation); main constituents menthol (40.7%) and menthone (23.4%).

56-041.r: Asafoetida (hing) → dried latex (oleo-gum resin) of Ferula plants (Umbelliferae), from rhizome and tap roots; bitumen and tincal are not plant products.

56-042.r: Opium → fruit; hing → root; rubber → stem; quinine → bark (cinchona).

56-043.r: Asafoetida (hing) → dried sap from the rhizome (modified stem) and fleshy tap roots of Ferula; endemic to Afghanistan, Iran. Book gives two answers: (a) and (b).

56-044.r: Quinine (anti-malaria drug) → stem bark of cinchona tree, an angiosperm; a white, bitter crystalline alkaloid.

56-049.r: Arteether (anti-malaria) → from a seeded plant, Artemisia annua. Malaria = Plasmodium parasite, spread by female Anopheles mosquito.

56-050.r: Quinine (cinchona bark) for malaria was replaced by the synthetic drug chloroquine.

56-051.r: Hydroxychloroquine and chloroquine are synthetic drugs, not from any plant; quinine comes from cinchona bark. The book gives no single answer (*) – question flawed.

56-052.r: Cork → bark of the cork oak, Quercus suber (native to the Mediterranean region).

56-053.r: Cotton → mainly cellulose (91.00%); water 7.85%, protoplasm 0.55%, mineral salts 0.20%.

56-055.r: Heroin → from opium poppy (Papaver somniferum): opium latex has about 12% morphine, chemically processed into heroin.

56-056.r: Morphine → from unripe fruits of poppy; a painkiller and sleeping drug acting on the CNS; name from Morpheus.

56-057.r: Opium → dried latex collected by making shallow cuts on unripe poppy fruit.

56-059.r: Main constituent of opium → morphine (about 12%), an alkaloid processed into heroin.

56-060.r: Opium plant → Papaver somniferum (family Papaveraceae); latex of immature capsules gives morphine, codeine, papaverine.

56-061.r: Opium → depressant (sedative) narcotic: slows heart rate and breathing, reduces pain; latex ≈ 12% morphine.

56-062.r: Narcotic analgesic (opioid) among options → morphine, a natural opium alkaloid used for severe pain.

56-063.r: Tapa (bark) cloth → soaked, beaten inner bark of Moraceae trees (mulberry, fig); not woven; made in Pacific islands like Samoa and Fiji.

56-064.r: Iodine → Laminaria (kelp), a brown seaweed; also rich in iron and potassium.

57-001.r: Pathogen → living microorganism that causes disease (virus, bacterium, protozoan, prion, viroid, fungus); also called infectious agents or germs.

57-002.r: Not true: 'DNA viruses are usually single-stranded' – they may be double- (dsDNA) or single-stranded (ssDNA). True: term by Beijerinck; RNA viruses mutate more.

57-003.r: Bacteriophage → virus that infects and multiplies in bacteria (and archaea); protein coat with DNA or RNA inside.

57-004.r: All three false: viruses abound in ocean water; bacteriophages infect bacteria; viruses can alter host-cell transcription → none correct.

57-005.r: Only 1 true: viruses lack energy-making enzymes, so cannot be grown in synthetic media; they spread by various means, not by vectors only.

57-006.r: Lichen, bacteria and algae have enzymes; viruses mostly use host enzymes, yet some carry a few → answer (e), 'None of the above'.

57-007.r: ACE2 (angiotensin-converting enzyme 2) → protein on cells of lungs, heart, kidneys etc.; discussed in the spread of viral diseases.

57-008.r: Coronaviruses (RNA viruses) cause SARS, MERS and COVID-19 → all of the above; milder ones cause some common colds.

57-009.r: COVID-19 pandemic → caused by SARS-CoV-2; outbreak began in Wuhan, China, in December 2019 and spread worldwide in early 2020.

57-010.r: Covishield (Oxford-AstraZeneca, made by Serum Institute, Pune) is not mRNA-based (1 false); Sputnik V → vector platform; Covaxin (Bharat Biotech, ICMR) → inactivated pathogen.

57-012.r: Covishield adult dose → 0.5 ml; it uses a weakened, non-replicating chimpanzee adenovirus engineered to make coronavirus proteins.

57-013.r: Sputnik V (Gam-COVID-Vac) → Russian adenovirus vector vaccine (Gamaleya Institute); registered 11 August 2020; Russia exported it to India.

57-014.r: Moderna → mRNA COVID-19 vaccine (USA): modified mRNA for the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein inside lipid nanoparticles; Sputnik V is an adenovirus vector vaccine.
57-014.t: Sinovac, Novavax and Sputnik are not mRNA vaccines; Moderna is.

57-015.r: COVID vaccines → none widely used is live attenuated: mRNA and viral-vector vaccines make cells produce harmless spike protein; Covaxin uses inactivated virus. Book's answer: (a).
57-015.c: BPSC's key also took live attenuated virus, but no widely used COVID vaccine is one: mRNA and vector vaccines (Covishield) make cells produce harmless spike protein, and Covaxin uses killed virus. Scientifically, (c) fits.

57-016.r: Viral vector vaccines → a modified, harmless different virus (vector) carries instructions for the disease virus's antigens into cells, triggering immunity.

57-017.r: Monoclonal antibodies → lab-made proteins mimicking natural antibodies; bind specific antigens to trigger immune function; used for viral infections like Nipah – all three true.

57-018.r: Wolbachia method → controls mosquito-borne viral diseases: Wolbachia bacteria (in 50-60% of insects) block dengue, chikungunya, Zika in Aedes aegypti.

57-019.r: Dengue ('breakbone fever') → virus spread by the bite of female Aedes mosquito (mainly Aedes aegypti).

57-022.r: Dengue → rapid fall in blood platelets, which can cause internal bleeding.

57-023.r: Only 3 true: dengue is viral, not protozoan; symptoms include retro-orbital pain (behind eyes), skin rash, bleeding from nose and gums.

57-024.r: Dengue → viral (Aedes mosquito), not bacterial; diphtheria, plague and pneumonia are bacterial (pneumonia can also be fungal or viral).

57-025.r: Yellow fever → viral disease spread by the bite of female Aedes aegypti mosquito, not by air, water or housefly → 'None of the above'.

57-026.r: Tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus) spreads yellow fever, dengue, chikungunya; Japanese encephalitis is spread by Culex mosquitoes.

57-027.r: Hydrophobia (fear of water) = old name of rabies, a viral disease that affects the nervous system.

57-028.r: Meningitis → inflammation of the meninges, the protective membranes over brain and spinal cord; caused by viruses, bacteria etc.

57-029.r: Rotavirus (double-stranded RNA, family Reoviridae) → commonest cause of severe diarrhoea in infants; kills one in every 200 babies born in India.

57-030.r: Pandemic → disease spread across a large region (countries, continents, world); epidemic → many cases in a short time; endemic → regularly found in one place.

57-031.r: All-viral set → mumps, rabies, herpes; other viral diseases: chickenpox, flu, HIV/AIDS, measles, poliomyelitis.

57-032.r: Poliovirus enters through polluted food and water (fecal-oral route); polio is a contagious viral infection that can cause paralysis.

57-034.r: Polio vaccine → Jonas Salk (book: 'Jones Salk'), 1952; poliovirus affects the central nervous system.

57-037.r: Polio: India, polio-free for five years, switched from trivalent OPV (types 1, 2, 3) to bivalent OPV (types 1 and 3).

57-038.r: Common cold → mainly rhinovirus, the most common viral infectious agent in humans.

57-039.r: Pneumonia → infection of the lungs: inflames air sacs, which may fill with fluid or pus; caused by viruses, bacteria or fungi.

57-040.r: Hepatitis B → blood-borne (blood, body fluids, mother to newborn), not water-borne; typhoid, jaundice and cholera are waterborne.

57-041.r: Hepatitis B → HBV, a partially double-stranded DNA virus (Hepadnaviridae); causes liver scarring, liver failure, liver cancer.

57-043.r: Not correct: 'Hepatitis B, unlike C, has no vaccine'. True: HBV spreads like HIV (blood, mother-to-baby, sex); hepatitis = liver inflammation by viruses A-E.

57-046.r: Wrong pair: polio – monkey (polio spreads person to person via faecal matter entering the mouth). Correct: plague – rat; rabies – dog; tapeworm – pig.

57-047.r: Only smallpox is eradicated in India (declared free 1977); diphtheria, chickenpox are not. Also: Guinea worm eradicated 2000; polio-free certificate 27 March 2014.

57-048.r: Smallpox (Variola major and minor) → WHO certified global eradication in 1980; last natural case was in October 1977.

57-049.r: Smallpox → variola virus, spread by droplets in close contact; patient rests on a separate bed → book: both true, reason based on assertion.

57-050.r: AIDS → caused by HIV, a virus, not bacteria; HIV infects T-helper cells and cripples immunity. Diphtheria, cholera, whooping cough are bacterial.

57-051.r: AIDS spreads by sexual contact, blood transfusion and across the placenta (1, 2, 4); not by mosquitoes, sneezing, coughing or kissing.

57-053.r: AIDS destroys T-4 lymphocytes (helper cells) of cell-mediated immunity → immune system fails; A and R true, R explains A.

57-054.r: AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome) → caused by HIV virus; symptoms: swollen lymph nodes, night sweats, memory loss, weight loss – all four.

57-060.r: HIV (a retrovirus) → RNA + protein: core holds two identical RNA genomes plus enzymes reverse transcriptase, protease, integrase.

57-061.r: Only 2 true: adenoviruses have double-stranded (not single) DNA and can cause common cold; AIDS virus (HIV) is a retrovirus.

57-063.r: Tattooing with unsterile equipment or ink can spread hepatitis B and HIV-AIDS (also hepatitis C, TB); chikungunya is not spread this way.

57-064.r: Dominant HIV strain in India → HIV 1C. HIV was first recognised in 1981 and has killed more than 25 million people.

57-065.r: HTLV-III (AIDS virus) was discovered by Robert Gallo (Institute of Human Virology, University of Maryland).

57-066.r: Most used AIDS medicine → zidovudine (book: 'Zedovudine'; azidothymidine), an anti-retroviral drug.

57-067.r: ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) → detects antibodies in blood; first widely used screening test for HIV/AIDS.

57-068.r: Japanese encephalitis → infection of the brain by JEV (a flavivirus), spread by mosquitoes; about 68,000 clinical cases a year in Asia.

57-070.r: Keeping pigs away from settlements helps eradicate Japanese encephalitis: pigs and wild birds are virus reservoirs; Culex mosquitoes spread it.

57-071.r: Antibiotics cannot cure measles (viral respiratory infection); leprosy, tetanus and cholera are bacterial and curable with antibiotics.

57-073.r: AIDS, chickenpox, mumps and herpes simplex are all infectious diseases. The book gives no single answer (*).

57-074.r: Ranikhet disease → highly infectious viral disease of chickens (poultry).

57-075.r: All four are infectious diseases of milch animals: foot and mouth (viral), anthrax (Bacillus anthracis), black quarter (Clostridium chauvoei), cowpox.

57-076.r: Foot and mouth disease → virus (Aphthovirus, family Picornaviridae) of cloven-hoofed animals: cattle, sheep, goat, pig.

57-078.r: Rinderpest (cattle plague; Morbillivirus) → declared eradicated in 2011, the first animal disease ever eliminated.

57-079.r: Bird flu (avian influenza) → H5N1 virus; mainly hens and ducks; spreads hen-to-man and man-to-man; Tamiflu blocks influenza A and B.

57-082.r: Swine flu → H1N1 virus, first detected in 2009 and called 'swine flu' as it resembled pig viruses; spreads among humans by coughing, sneezing.
57-082.t: Don't confuse H1N1 (swine flu) with H5N1 (bird flu).

57-083.r: Both true: Zika spreads by Aedes mosquitoes (mainly Aedes aegypti), the same that carry dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever; sexual transmission is also possible.

57-084.r: Wrong pair: Ebola virus – smallpox (Ebola causes Ebola haemorrhagic fever). Correct: biometrics – fingerprints, iris; cloning – genetic replica; DNA fingerprinting – paternity.

57-085.r: Ebola → deadly virus first found in 1976 near the Ebola river, Democratic Republic of Congo; named after that river.

57-087.r: Nipah virus outbreak → Kerala (Kozhikode), May-June 2018, 17 deaths; it returned in 2021 and 2024.

58-001.r: Food poisoning → Salmonella bacteria (also cause typhoid, gastroenteritis); infection mostly through contaminated water or food.
